v_hook: Tests sample. Laws prove. And now, proofs carry certificates. This is what is new in T S laws, version one.
v_mono: First, monorepos. Every package owns its laws, its config, its approvers and its accept flow. One GitHub flow covers the whole repo. In VS Code, the project follows whichever file you have open.
v_changed: Run check from the root and each project reports under its own header. Add changed, and only the affected projects run, picked through the dependency graph. I changed core. U I and web depend on it, so they run. Docs does not, so it is skipped. A big repo stays fast, and nothing that depends on your change is missed.
v_cert: Second, proof certificates. A proved result used to mean you trusted the solver. Now cvc5 writes an Alethe proof of the answer, and Carcara, a separate checker, verifies it. Two programs have to agree before a law says certified.
v_cert_real: This is real output from our C I job, with cvc5 one point four point two and Carcara. Straight line big integer and boolean laws come out certified. Loop proofs report uncertified, because the loop solver writes no proof to check. So does a proof Carcara rejects, and one that needs a rewrite rule cvc5 does not define. I would rather show you that than hide it.
v_cert_bind: A certificate is checked again at accept, and the lock binds it to the exact problem, with hashes of the problem, the proof and the checker. Edit the law and the certificate is void. Set certify to require, and a proof with no certificate fails the check. That includes every loop proof, so require only suits projects that stay in the straight line.
v_loops: Third, loop invariants. Z three Spacer finds the invariant through constrained Horn clauses, and plain Z three checks it again. Eldarica or Golem can cross check, when you have them installed. Arrays of any length work too. A loop is proved for every input, not just the ones a test tried.
v_loops_real: Here is the real thing. The invariant is printed beside the law, so you can read what was proved about the loop, even though it carries no certificate yet.
v_sec: Fourth, security laws, mapped to their C W E. Path traversal, prototype pollution, open redirect, regular expression denial of service, cross site scripting, integer issues and input validation. This sanitiser strips dot dot slash, and the law finds the payload that walks straight past it. The one that resolves the path and checks it is only tested here, and the report says so.
v_deps: And T S laws security deps checks the packages your covered code imports against O S V. Old lodash and minimist fail with their advisories and the version that fixes them. In C I, run it with no cache, so every run asks again.
v_accept: Fifth, accepting laws. Locally, a person at a terminal accepts. In a GitHub project you can also accept on demand, with a manual run of the merge workflow. The person who starts it needs maintain access, and the run has to still be at the head of the branch. If the branch moved, it accepts nothing and says so.
v_oidc: Last, how it ships. Publishing uses O I D C trusted publishing. The release job asks GitHub for a short lived identity, npm trusts that workflow, and every package carries provenance. There are no npm tokens to leak.
v_outro: T S laws one point oh. Install it, write a law, and let the proofs show their working. npm i dash D tslaws.
